source_title: Beat the Market: An Effective Intraday Momentum Strategy for S&P500 ETF (SPY) — Zarattini, Aziz & Barbon (2024)
bull_case: The paper builds 'noise bands' from the 14-day typical intraday move at each point in the day (exactly our noise_z feature) and goes long/short on a breakout through them, exiting on a VWAP trailing stop. Backtested 2007–early 2024 it returned 1,985% net of costs (19.6%/yr, Sharpe 1.33), and an independent GitHub replication confirmed the effect out-of-sample (Sharpe 1.11, alpha +16.7%/yr, t=2.85, cross-validated against ES futures with 0.97 correlation) — a rare case of a published intraday rule surviving a skeptical third-party replication with real walk-forward testing.
bear_case: The same replication found the Sharpe had decayed to roughly 0 on both SPY and ES futures by 2025, and that further parameter optimization (27-variant grid, walk-forward) destroyed value rather than improved it — a textbook post-publication decay pattern. Our one-shot daily translation (single 10:30 check, fixed stop, hold-to-close) also drops the continuous VWAP trailing-stop that drove much of the original edge, so the version we can actually encode is a simplification of the simplification.

reasons: noise_z maps almost exactly onto the paper's own normalized breakout signal, so translation risk is low
decay was documented post-2024; our search window (pre-2021 thresholds) likely predates the crowding
independent replication with real stats is stronger evidence than a typical blog backtest

source_title: Can Day Trading Really Be Profitable? Evidence from Opening Range Breakout (ORB) Day Trading — Zarattini & Aziz (2023)
bull_case: The rule is simple and mechanical: trade in the direction of the first 5-minute candle, stop at its opposite extreme, target 10x the risk or the close. Over 2016–2023 on QQQ it returned 1,484% vs. 169% buy-and-hold; a later independent replication across five indices found the first-candle-direction edge was 'small but real' against a random-direction benchmark and survived out of sample in four of five indices.
bear_case: The original paper charges commission only (no spread or slippage) and has no true out-of-sample period, so its headline numbers overstate what's tradeable. Our earliest allowed decision point is 30 minutes after the open, not 5 minutes — by 10:00 much of the information content of the 'first candle' has likely already been arbitraged into price, so ret_open at m=30 is a materially slower, weaker proxy for the original signal.

reasons: directional edge was replicated across multiple indices with real stats, not just the original sample
mechanism (early momentum carrying into the close) is economically simple and doesn't require data-mined conditioning
translation to a 30-min checkpoint is a real but bounded fidelity loss, worth testing rather than assuming it fails

source_title: Market Intraday Momentum — Gao, Han, Li & Zhou
bull_case: One of the most replicated findings in the intraday literature: the return from yesterday's close to 10:00am (our ret_prev_close at m=30) predicts the last half-hour return with the same sign, R²=1.6%, both statistically and economically significant over 1993-2013, and stronger on higher-volume days (hence the vol_ratio filter, which is the paper's own conditioning result, not an invented add-on). A simple long-when-positive, hold-to-close version was independently re-tested recently and reported ~6.67%/yr annualized.
bear_case: The core sample is old (pre-2013) and intraday predictability of this kind is exactly the sort of pattern that tends to get arbitraged away as algorithmic participation grows; R²=1.6% is small. It also sits conceptually close to the lab's already-heavily-tested gap/prev_day_ret continuation family, though the exact feature (ret_prev_close, cumulative since yesterday's close) and hold-to-close exit differ from what's been tried.

reasons: long, independently-replicated academic track record with a known effect size and direction
single trade/day with hold-to-close keeps turnover and cost exposure minimal
volume filter is drawn directly from the paper's own finding, not a data-mined addition

bull_case: This is the most-cited recent (2023) empirical paper on day trading: buying/selling QQQ at the break of the first few minutes' range and holding to the close reportedly returned 1,484% (2016-2023) vs 169% buy-and-hold, with a defined stop at the opposite side of the opening range. range_pos>p90 at the first 30-minute mark is a faithful proxy for 'breaking to the top of the opening range.'

The original paper's headline return also depended on 3-4x leverage, which is unavailable/unmodeled here, and ORB is now a widely-marketed retail strategy (crowding risk).

Using a 3-condition, each-at-p90 filter here will also produce very few trades over the 2016-2020 search window.

source_title: Gao, Han, Li & Zhou — "Intraday Momentum: The First Half-Hour Return Predicts the Last Half-Hour Return" (SPY ETF, 1993-2013)
bull_case: The paper's core, replicated finding is that the SPY return measured from yesterday's close through 10:00 (i.e. gap + first 30 min) predicts the direction of the rest of the day, with R²≈1.6% (comparable to monthly-frequency predictability elsewhere in finance), statistically significant in and out of sample, and strongest on high-volume/high-volatility days — which is why I gate on vol_ratio>p60 as the paper itself documents the effect concentrates there.
bear_case: This is one of the most famous and most crowded intraday anomalies in the literature (cited hundreds of times, built into commercial products), so it is a prime crowding/decay candidate; follow-up work I found explicitly notes the first-half/last-half correlation has flipped negative in more recent (2021+) samples. It also has conceptual overlap with the lab's heavily-explored 'gap' family of specs, since ret_prev_close at 10:00 is just gap plus the first 30 minutes of trading.

reasons: Mechanism and feature map cleanly onto ret_prev_close + vol_ratio, which is exactly how the paper defines its own moderating condition
Hold-to-close, single round trip, so cost drag is low relative to the ~1.6% R² reported
Decay risk is real (post-2021 sign flip reported elsewhere) but the 2016-2020 search window predates most of the reported decay
Distinct from the lab's gap-only combos since it requires the move to persist through the first half hour, not just an overnight gap

source_title: Independent replication of Zarattini, Aziz & Barbon (2024/2025) "Beat the Market: An Effective Intraday Momentum Strategy for S&P500 ETF (SPY)"
bull_case: The paper builds a volatility-normalized 'noise band' around the open (average absolute deviation from open over the prior 14 days, by minute-of-day) and trades breakouts beyond it — this is literally the construction of the lab's own noise_z feature, so it's a very direct, well-matched translation. It also overlaps partially with the lab's existing best QQQ-10:00 idea (ret_30-based), so some of any measured edge may just be a restatement of already-explored search space.

reasons: Mechanism (range-position breakout + stop/target to close) is distinct enough from the existing best QQQ-10:00 idea (which used rv_5d/vol_ratio filters, not range_pos) to be worth an independent run

source_title: Using Internal Bar Strength as a Key Indicator for Trading Country ETFs
bull_case: IBS = (close-low)/(high-low) is a well-documented mean-reversion factor for equity ETFs (original Pagonidis NAAIM paper, reproduced on country ETFs in this arXiv paper): a close near the day's low tends to be followed by a bounce. prev_day_ibs is a fresh feature for this lab (absent from the best-ideas list and the recent-trials sample), it's known with zero lookahead at the open, and a single clean percentile condition gives plenty of trades (~15% of days) with a long hold-to-close that minimizes cost drag.
bear_case: The documented effect is a close-to-next-close (overnight) trade; our same-day-only version only captures whatever part of the reversion happens intraday after 10:00, which may be the smaller, noisier remainder once the open has already partly reflected it. The original evidence is strongest on less-liquid country ETFs, which may not transfer to a heavily arbitraged, high-volume index product like QQQ.

reasons: single, well-documented factor not yet explored by the lab (new feature)
fully known-at-decision-time, no lookahead
plenty of trade frequency at q15
faithful but partial translation of an overnight effect into an intraday-only rule is an honest, bounded simplification

source_title: Fading the Gap: How Large Overnight Moves in SPY and QQQ Play Out During the Trading Day

Adding prev_day_ibs<q30 narrows the entry to days that also closed weak the prior session (a 'capitulation' context), which the source doesn't test but is a reasonable refinement in the same direction as its evidence.

The lab's own best-ideas cluster has already heavily explored gap-based SPY setups (albeit gap-UP continuation, not gap-DOWN reversal), so there's real risk this whole feature family is close to exhausted.

source_title: Opening Range Breakout Research: What Two Day-Trading Papers Actually Found
bull_case: Summarizing Zarattini/Barbon/Aziz (2024, 2025), the unfiltered opening-range-breakout edge was weak (29% vs 198% benchmark over the test period) but filtering for abnormally high relative volume turned it into the dominant driver of returns (1,637% in the equities study), and the QQQ-specific follow-up paper confirms the same breakout-continuation mechanism with large asymmetric targets (10R). range_pos>q80 proxies 'making a new high within today's range' and vol_ratio>q70 proxies the relative-volume filter that was the key to both papers' results.
bear_case: Both papers use a 5-minute opening range and ATR-scaled stops on thousands of names (or QQQ/TQQQ with no slippage modeled); our 60-minute decision point and coarse range_pos/vol_ratio percentiles are a much blunter instrument than what drove the published results, and the lab's own learned weights already tag range_pos as a feature that 'tends to hurt'. A target_r of 4 will get stopped out on most chop days, making the result sensitive to a few large winners (fragile tail-dependence).

reasons: mechanism (relative-volume-confirmed breakout) is concretely documented across two recent papers
feature combo not present in the lab's recent-trials sample
known risk of tail-dependence is manageable via the fold-based scoring

source_title: Mean Reversion Strategy: +40% SPY While Others Took the Loss
bull_case: Internal Bar Strength (IBS = (close-low)/(high-low)) mean reversion is one of the longest-documented equity-ETF anomalies (Pagonidis 2014 NAAIM paper), and the piece I read reports it still backtests at +40% on SPY (2.85% drawdown) and +45% on QQQ with high win rates, suggesting persistence across decades. A weak prior-day close near the day's low (low IBS) plausibly reflects late-day forced selling/capitulation that partially reverses the next session, which prev_day_ibs captures exactly as specified in our grammar.

My SPY/close-exit variant is a thin re-skin of that same idea (different market, p10 vs p15, exit close vs hold240) and the instructions explicitly say not to repeat already-tried ideas. IBS is also one of the most widely publicized mean-reversion indicators on retail quant blogs since 2014, raising real crowding/decay concerns for liquid index ETFs specifically.

source_title: Opening Range Breakout for Stocks in Play
bull_case: This QuantConnect research piece reports a volume-confirmed opening-range breakout (defining 'in play' via first-5-minute volume vs. its 14-day average, almost exactly our vol_ratio feature) achieving a 2.396 Sharpe vs. 0.836 for SPY buy-and-hold, with a defined ATR-based stop. Requiring both a breakout (range_pos near the day's high) and confirming volume is a sensible filter: it should screen out low-conviction breakouts that fade, which is the classic complaint about plain ORB.
bear_case: I read this page in full: the strategy explicitly operates on a cross-sectional universe (top 20 of the 1,000 most liquid US stocks ranked by relative volume each day) and the authors of a related study note 'the stock-selection filter does most of the work' — i.e. the edge comes from picking which stocks are unusually active that day, a mechanism that doesn't exist for a single always-traded ETF like SPY. Separately, independent replications of the closely-related Zarattini/Barbon/Aziz 5-minute ORB paper found the edge had thinned to about $0.04/trade pre-cost in 2016-2023 data and collapsed post-2021 — directly overlapping our 2016-2020 search window and beyond.

reasons: Core alpha mechanism (cross-sectional stock selection) does not transfer to a single-ETF implementation

source_title: First and Last Half Hours of Trading Linked?
bull_case: The classic Gao-Han-Xie-Zhou (JFE 2018) finding is that SPY's first half-hour return (9:30-10:00) predicts its last half-hour return, with the original 1999-2012 out-of-sample test showing 6.3% annualized vs -0.5% for buy-and-hold by simply holding into the close when the first half hour was positive. It's a clean, well-cited, mechanically simple signal that maps directly onto our ret_30 feature at the first decision time.
bear_case: The CXO Advisory follow-up I read already showed material decay by 2014 (R² dropped from 0.018 to 0.014, correlation only 0.12), and a 2025-26 independent replication I found explicitly re-tested this exact anomaly across 7 instruments and reported it 'does not replicate out of sample... β₁ is negative on all 7 instruments,' with 0 of 19 significant in-development specifications surviving the holdout. This is about as direct a 'this idea is dead' signal as exists for any item on this list, and ret_30-based specs are also already heavily explored by this lab (QQQ ret_30/rv_5d/vol_ratio combo is the current best QQQ idea) in a different, better-performing configuration.

source_title: The End-of-Day Reversal After 2019: A Pre-Registered Test on S&P 500 Stocks Excluding Heavily Traded Names
bull_case: This 2026 pre-registered study tests whether intraday 'winners' (stocks near their daily high, proxied here by range_pos) reverse against intraday 'losers' over the final 30 minutes of trading, a pattern with roots in classic late-day reversal/inventory-risk literature (market makers unwinding positions into the close).
bear_case: I read the abstract directly: the authors pre-registered this test specifically to check whether the reversal survives post-2019, and found it does not for large-cap names — the effect fell from 3.40bp (2016-2019) to just 0.74bp (2023-2026) on the full S&P 500 index, with the authors explicitly attributing the residual effect to smaller constituents after excluding ~80 heavily-traded mega-cap stocks. SPY and QQQ are themselves baskets dominated by exactly those excluded mega-cap names, so this is close to a direct statement that the effect we'd be testing is already known to be dead in our instruments.

source_title: Zarattini intraday momentum on the Nasdaq: long survives, short is a mirage
bull_case: This is a direct translation of the Zarattini/Aziz/Barbon 'noise area' breakout (SSRN 4824172, 'Beat the Market', 2007-2024 SPY) onto QQQ/Nasdaq-100: boundaries = open price times (1 ± average |return| from open at that minute over the last 14 days); breaking the upper boundary signals a genuine demand imbalance. The independent 2026 Nasdaq-100 futures replication I read confirms the long side specifically (not just the original SPY result) survived a true out-of-sample split (parameters locked on 2010-2017, tested 2018-2026): business-day Sharpe 0.90 in-sample vs 0.68 out-of-sample, 6 of 9 OOS years positive. The authors also report the edge is stronger when realized/implied vol is elevated, which rv_5d>p50 proxies.
bear_case: The underlying paper and its replications use a dynamic 14-day rolling noise band and a VWAP trailing stop checked every 30 minutes intraday; my spec freezes the threshold as a fixed 2016-2020 percentile of noise_z and substitutes a flat 50bp stop for the VWAP trailing stop, which is a real simplification that could change the risk profile. The strategy is now well-publicized (multiple SSRN papers, GitHub replications, newsletter writeups since 2024), raising crowding risk, and 'noise_z' combos have already been tried by this lab in other directions (e.g. SPY 11:00 noise_z<p94 combos) without reward, so there's some feature fatigue risk even though this exact long-only/high-vol-regime framing hasn't been tried.

reasons: Recent (2018-2026) out-of-sample replication on a different but closely related index (Nasdaq-100) specifically validates the long side, addressing look-ahead/overfitting concerns better than most ORB-style papers
rv_5d filter is grounded in the original paper's own VIX-regime robustness check, not a mined addition
Lab has not tested a pure noise_z breakout long with a vol-regime filter at this decision time/exit combo

source_title: Fading the Gap: How Large Overnight Moves in SPY and QQQ Play Out During the Trading Day
bull_case: The piece documents, with concrete SPY/QQQ statistics, that QQQ gap-ups of 1%+ fade intraday more than SPY does: average open-to-close drift of -0.5% versus -0.2%, with the intraday high averaging only +0.9% above the open before fading to a -1.8% low. This lines up with the academic overnight/intraday reversal literature (Akbas et al. 2022) that positive overnight returns tend to be followed by negative daytime reversals in US equities, giving the pattern a plausible economic story (overnight order flow from retail/futures markets overshoots, specialists/market makers absorb and mean-revert it during the session).
bear_case: The same research thread I found notes a 'structural break' in gap-fade strategies from 2022 onward, with equity curves peaking in H1 2022 and giving back gains afterward — i.e. exactly the kind of regime change that would hurt a spec calibrated on 2016-2020 percentiles and tested through more recent folds. The shareplanner numbers are raw, non-cost-adjusted averages across all gap-ups, not a backtested rule with a hold-to-close/stop structure, so the translation into this spec is a faithful but real simplification. Gap is already a feature the lab has used extensively (in the long-continuation SPY 11:00 cluster), so the model may already be 'full' on gap information in the other direction.

reasons: Average documented effect size (-50bp to -180bp) is an order of magnitude bigger than the 2bp round-trip cost, so it isn't a knife's-edge cost story
Short-gap-fade on QQQ specifically (vs. the lab's existing long gap-continuation cluster on SPY) is a genuinely different, untried direction/market combination
Decision is made at a fixed time using only pre-open information (gap), so no look-ahead

bull_case: Zarattini & Aziz (2023) report that being long QQQ whenever price is above session VWAP and short whenever below (reversing on every VWAP cross) turned $25k into $192,656 (671%) net of commissions, 2018-2023, Sharpe 2.1, max drawdown only 9.4% — a clean, mechanically simple directional rule with a real economic rationale (VWAP as a running consensus price).
bear_case: A direct replication found the published numbers only hold with zero slippage. Adding a single tick of realistic slippage collapses QQQ Sharpe from 1.91 to 0.10 and return from +458% to +1% (TQQQ falls to -99%), because the true edge averages ~2.5 cents/share spread across ~40,000 fills over six years — the 'edge' is smaller than normal transaction costs. Our grammar's 1bp/side cost and single-fixed-time entry is a weak proxy for a strategy whose published edge depended on continuous re-entry and was already shown to be a cost artifact.

Even CXO's own 2012-2014 update already found the effect shrinking toward magnitudes too small to trade after costs, years before the more recent inversion.

Second read: both inputs (rv_5d, range_pos) are already in the lab's feature set and flagged as roughly neutral, so this specific combination (low vol + range breakout, rather than gap or prev-day features) hasn't been directly tried together.
bear_case: First read: the source I actually read is entirely qualitative — it gives a 4-step narrative ('identify contraction', 'wait for breakout', 'enter at acceptance') with zero quantitative thresholds, win rates, or backtest numbers anywhere in the article, despite searching specifically for statistics. Second read: 'volatility compression precedes expansion' is almost tautological (it's definitionally true that very low vol periods are eventually followed by higher vol, in either direction) and says nothing about directional edge or whether the expansion is profitable net of costs — this is the kind of plausible-sounding, unfalsified pattern most likely to fail once actually tested.

reasons: Zero quantitative evidence in the source — purely narrative technical-analysis folklore
The underlying claim (compression precedes expansion) doesn't actually imply directional profitability, only higher variance, which this spec's long-only framing doesn't account for

source_title: A Profitable Day Trading Strategy For The U.S. Equity Market (Zarattini & Aziz, SSRN 4416622/4729284, 2023)
bull_case: First read: the paper finds that QQQ's return in the opening minutes predicts the direction and persistence of the rest of the day — buy when the opening range breaks up, hold to the close, stop at the other side of the range — and reports a 33% annualized alpha net of commissions over 2016-2023, a result independently replicated on GitHub (giovannibrusco/zarattini-2023-orb-qqq) with a significant t-stat even after stress-testing execution costs. Second read: the mechanism (informed order flow concentrated at the open, momentum before mean-reversion sets in) is plausible and long-standing in market-microstructure literature, and QQQ's single-name concentration (mega-cap tech) gives it more persistent opening order imbalances than SPY.
bear_case: First read: the original rule uses a 5-minute opening range re-entered at the 10-minute mark; our grammar's earliest decision point is 30 minutes, so this is a materially slower, coarser version of the published edge and may not capture the same effect at all. Second read: the independent replication itself found execution-cost break-even at ~2.2c/share slippage, and a related NQ-confirmation variant lost money in 2023 and underperformed buy-and-hold by ~3x in another critique — so the published headline number looks fragile outside the exact paper specification, and ORB-style ideas are now widely known/crowded since 2023.

reasons: Real, specific, independently-replicated mechanism distinct from everything in the lab's tried list (uses ret_30+range_pos as an opening-range-breakout proxy, not gap/prev_day_ret)
30-minute decision point is a faithful-but-slower simplification of a 5-minute rule, so expect a weaker effect than published — worth one test to see if it survives at all
Known fragility to costs in replications, so treat any positive result cautiously

source_title: Internal Bar Strength for Mean Reversion — Alvarez Quant Trading
bull_case: First read: Internal Bar Strength — where yesterday's close sat in yesterday's range, exactly our prev_day_ibs feature — is one of the longest-standing, most independently-replicated mean-reversion signals in equities; the article itself documents a clean monotonic relationship (win rate 71% when IBS is near 0 vs 57% near 100) even on single names, and the effect's originator (Pagonidis, NAAIM, titled explicitly 'The IBS Effect: Mean Reversion in Equity ETFs') and several independent write-ups report large multi-decade SPY backtests (e.g. ~12.7% CAGR, 0.97 Sharpe, 69% win rate since 1993). Second read: the signal is known before the open (no lookahead), is slow-moving/structural (tied to selling exhaustion), and is one of the few effects the lab hasn't tried via prev_day_ibs as the sole driver — the closest the lab has run is a random evolution trial shorting high IBS, the opposite bet.
bear_case: First read: the article I actually read tests individual S&P 500 stocks, not the SPY/QQQ index ETFs themselves — the SPY-specific numbers come from secondary blog sources I could not fully verify by reading a clean page (bot-walled), so there's a real risk the magnitude doesn't transfer to the ETF level. reasons: Multiple independent sources over a decade converge on the same sign and rough magnitude specifically for SPY, giving more confidence than a single backtest

source_title: The Gap Map: When US Equity Gaps Continue, Fade, and Mean Nothing
bull_case: Directly fetched and read: across 6,552 overnight-gap events in SPY/QQQ/IWM/NVDA/TSLA/AAPL from Jan 2022-May 2026, the authors report mid-size up-gaps (1-2%) are 'the only band where continuation beats coin-flip (53.7%)' with median drift +0.11%, and that 'the highest-quality continuation evidence shows up between roughly 09:45 and 10:30' -- i.e. deciding around 10:00 and holding ~60 minutes is exactly the window they found strongest. Large gaps (>2%) explicitly do NOT extend (50.5%, 'the day is mostly done'), so bounding the gap to a moderate band rather than taking any gap > p85 (as the lab has repeatedly tried) targets the specific bucket the source says has edge.
bear_case: This is a practitioner blog, not peer-reviewed; 53.7% vs 50% is a thin edge that may not survive 1bp/side costs on a 60-min hold. The authors themselves warn 'gap and go... stopped working' post-2020 because large gaps are now driven by 'overnight options expiry, ETF rebalances' rather than information -- the same structural shift could be thinning out the mid-size bucket too, just with a lag. The lab has already run many gap>p85 variants on SPY that scored ~0 reward, so there's a real chance moderate gaps are just as arbitraged away; the q70-q90 band is also a narrower band so trade count could run low (a known top rejection reason: 'too few trades').

reasons: Source gives a specific, recent (2022-2026), sample-sized (6,552 events) statistic for exactly this gap bucket and time window, read directly rather than inferred
Different market (QQQ) and parameterization (bounded moderate gap band, 60-min hold, no target) than anything in the lab's SPY gap>p85/hold-240 cluster
Edge is thin so must be scored net of costs, but that is what the backtest will do

source_title: Trend Day Trading Strategy: Maximizing One-Sided Markets
bull_case: Directly fetched: the article's five 'trend day' clues to check by 10:30am are price staying on one side of VWAP, shallow pullbacks, volume 'heavy, and heavier on moves than on dips', clean higher-highs/higher-lows, and one-sided internals -- i.e. persistent above-VWAP positioning plus elevated volume, exactly vwap_dist and vol_ratio. Their own (disclosed-as-simulated) stats show holding a confirmed trend day to the close returns +3.47R vs +1.46R for a fixed 2R target, and a false signal only costs -0.52R, needing just 13% accuracy to break even -- a favorable asymmetry if the signal has any real hit rate.
bear_case: The authors explicitly state 'R figures come from a DayTradingToolkit simulation, not live trading results,' so the favorable asymmetry is a modeling assumption, not an observed track record -- real slippage and gap risk on the stop could erode it. Trend days are also rare (~10-12% of sessions per trend-day literature generally), so this filter may trigger too few trades per the lab's dominant rejection reason. vol_ratio is listed as a feature that has been roughly neutral/mixed in the lab so far.

reasons: Mechanism (persistent above-VWAP + volume confirmation by mid-morning) is a coherent, commonly-cited trend-day signature read directly from source, not inferred
Distinct feature pairing (vwap_dist + vol_ratio only, no gap/prev_day terms) and market/time (QQQ, 11:00) from anything in the lab's current best-idea list

bull_case: Same directly-read source, different bucket: 'Small gaps (-0.5% to +0.5%) show median intraday return is positive - roughly +0.04% to +0.14%,' which the authors attribute to a 'structural bid in liquid US equities on calm tape.' That is direct evidence that fading (not following) a large early SPY move and holding toward the close has been the historically correct side in the recent sample, which is what this spec does using noise_z (a volatility-normalized version of the early return) as the trigger.

The 1993-2013 original finding and the 2021-2026 reversal could both be artifacts of regime-specific positioning (e.g., 0DTE options flow) that might itself be unstable going forward. noise_z (open-to-now move size-adjusted) is a proxy for, not identical to, the paper's raw first-half-hour return, so the mapping is approximate.

reasons: Grounded in a specific, recent (2021-2026), SPY-specific statistic (t=-2.3) read directly from source, documenting an actual reversal rather than assuming decay
Uses a feature (noise_z) and direction (short, fading strength) not yet tried together in the lab's trial history

A single-ETF, long-only, same-day version may behave differently, but the directional evidence that this specific signal has stopped working recently is hard to ignore.

source_title: Opening Range Breakout for Stocks in Play
bull_case: This writeup documents a mechanical opening-range breakout: long when price breaks above the opening range high on above-average volume, exit at close or on an ATR-based stop, reporting Sharpe 2.396 vs buy-and-hold's 0.836 with near-zero beta. range_pos>p85 (price near the top of the range established so far by 10:00) combined with vol_ratio>p60 (the volume-confirmation filter the paper emphasizes for 'stocks in play') is a faithful single-ETF translation.
bear_case: The reported Sharpe 2.4 is for a universe of abnormally-active individual stocks selected in real time ('stocks in play'), not a single fixed index ETF — applying the same rule to QQQ, which rarely has the kind of extreme relative-volume spikes the original strategy exploits, is a meaningful basis-risk gap. A separate, rigorous 2026 falsification study of OHLCV-based intraday momentum signals in futures (arXiv 2605.04004) found that most such signals (opening-range/volume-based included) fail to clear trading-cost hurdles once tested with proper statistical rigor across years, which is a relevant general caution here.

reasons: Concrete, fully-understood mechanical rule with a volume-confirmation filter distinct from the range_pos-only variants already tried and rejected in this lab
Known basis-risk (stock-selection universe vs fixed ETF) and a published falsification study both argue for caution, but the combination is still cheap and informative to test
Decision at 10:00 only uses range/volume information available by then

source_title: Hedging Demand and Market Intraday Momentum (Baltussen, Da, Lammers, Martens; JFE 2021)
bull_case: The paper examines 60+ futures across four decades (1974-2020) and finds the day's cumulative return up to late afternoon positively predicts the final-30-minute return, driven by gamma/delta-hedging rebalancing from option market makers and leveraged ETF issuers who must trade in the direction of the day's move right before the close. Crucially the authors show the effect is STRONGER where leveraged-ETF assets are large relative to the underlying - which describes QQQ (TQQQ/SQQQ, QLD/QID etc. are huge relative to QQQ's ADV) especially well, and this flow has only grown as leveraged-ETF AUM has ballooned since 2021, so the mechanism argument is a 'getting stronger' story rather than a decaying one. First pass: mechanism is structural (mandatory daily rebalancing), not just a statistical pattern, which is the strongest kind of argument for persistence. The lab's own feature weights already show the closest analogue, z_20d (daily oversold distance), is one of its weakest features (0.70), consistent with this family not working in this lab's own data.

reasons: Source's own honest re-test shows the edge is regime-dependent and negative-after-costs in choppy markets
Strategy is fundamentally a multi-day daily-hold mean-reversion rule, a poor fit for a single-session intraday translation
Lab's own weights show the closest related feature (z_20d, daily oversold) is already among the weakest tested (0.70)

reason: risk review: Source explicitly states there is no reliable published win rate or performance evidence for this exact setup; Pure mean-reversion against an extended move, with a tight stop and short hold - a high-churn, thin-edge profile; No independent confirmation found elsewhere beyond anecdotal trader guides
source_title: VWAP Mean Reversion: Intraday Rules, Stops, and Exits
bull_case: The guide describes a standard VWAP-fade setup: price stretched 2 standard deviations below session VWAP, then entering long on the first close back toward VWAP, stopped below the stretch low, targeting VWAP. Requiring range_pos to already be rising (price off today's low) before entering is a reasonable intraday-only simplification of 'first later close back above the lower band.'
bear_case: The source is explicit and unusually honest that 'there is no reliable published win rate' for this exact 2-std VWAP fade with a flat-at-close exit - it is a heuristic, not an evidenced strategy, and the only academic citation (Berkowitz/Logue/Noser 1988) is about VWAP as an execution benchmark, not a trading signal. A 25bp stop on a mean-reversion long in a 30-minute window is tight relative to typical SPY intraday noise, and fighting an extended move with no documented edge magnitude is risky against a 2x-cost bar.

reasons: Source explicitly states there is no reliable published win rate or performance evidence for this exact setup
Pure mean-reversion against an extended move, with a tight stop and short hold - a high-churn, thin-edge profile
No independent confirmation found elsewhere beyond anecdotal trader guides

source_title: Opening Range Breakout for Stocks in Play (implements Zarattini/Barbon/Aziz 2024 SSRN 4729284)
bull_case: The underlying paper reports a 2.4 Sharpe for the 5-minute ORB when restricted to names with abnormally high relative volume ('stocks in play'), vs 0.84 for buy-and-hold, with beta near zero. The mechanism (early breakout + confirming volume = informed order flow) is name-agnostic, so it should transfer from the paper's stock universe to SPY itself. rvol_30 is also independently flagged as a helpful feature by the lab's own 40k-trial history (weight 1.45).
bear_case: The paper's edge came from ranking the whole liquid-stock universe by relative volume and trading only the top 20 names each day; applying the same rvol threshold to SPY alone (which rarely has 'abnormal' volume relative to itself) may not reproduce the effect. The paper's reported win rate is only ~17%, so returns are carried by a few large winners - a style that is fragile to 2x cost tests and to regime change since the 2024 publication (crowding risk from a popular SSRN paper).

reasons: Source reports Sharpe 2.4 / beta~0 for ORB + relative-volume filter, a mechanism-based (not purely statistical) edge
rvol_30 is independently confirmed helpful in the lab's own learned feature weights (1.45)
Single EOD exit keeps the spec simple and distinct from the lab's existing gap-based winners
Moderate thresholds (q80/q70) should clear the lab's 150-trade minimum

source_title: Paper Review: An Effective Intraday Momentum Strategy (review of Zarattini/Aziz/Barbon, 'Beat the Market: An Effective Intraday Momentum Strategy for SPY', SSRN 4824172)
bull_case: The paper computes 'noise boundaries' each minute as the open times (1 +/- average daily return up to that minute over the last 14 days) - this is exactly the grammar's noise_z feature (return since open divided by its typical size over 14 days). Breaking outside the band signals demand/supply imbalance; the paper reports ~2000% cumulative return 2007-2024 and Sharpe above 1.3, performing best in high-VIX regimes. noise_z has essentially zero trial history in the lab yet (absent from both the helps and hurts lists), so this is genuinely unexplored territory.
bear_case: The published strategy uses continuous vol-targeted leverage (up to 4x) and a VWAP trailing-stop exit, neither of which the grammar's fixed stop/target/hold structure reproduces faithfully - our simplification could understate or overstate the real edge. The paper is from the same author trio as the ORB paper above, so a large share of today's proposals lean on one research group's methodology, raising shared data-snooping risk if their general approach doesn't hold up.

reasons: Direct feature match between the grammar's noise_z and the paper's noise-band formula - a faithful, not approximate, translation
Strong out-of-sample length in the original paper (2007-2024, 17 years) reduces single-period overfitting concern
Untested feature in the lab's history, diversifying away from the gap/ret_30/rvol_30 cluster that dominates current winners
Testing on QQQ (paper only used SPY) checks whether the effect generalizes

source_title: Do Volume Spikes Confirm Momentum (PyQuantLab)
bull_case: The article's core claim - that a relative-volume spike (current volume vs 20-day average, >1.5-2x) occurring alongside positive price momentum signals informed, continuing order flow, with exit on momentum reversal - is a direct, mechanism-based analogue of the grammar's rvol_30 + ret_30 combination. Both component features are independently confirmed helpful in the lab's own 40k-trial history (rvol_30 weight 1.45, ret_30 weight 1.66), giving two independent lines of evidence for the same combination.
bear_case: The source article itself reports no backtested performance numbers at all - it is a conceptual/code write-up, not an evidenced study, so the 'bull case' rests on plausibility rather than a demonstrated track record. Afternoon (13:00) relative-volume spikes could also just reflect pre-close positioning noise rather than genuine informed flow, and a 1-hour hold exposes the trade to mid-afternoon chop.

reasons: rvol_30 and ret_30 are each independently confirmed helpful by the lab's own learned weights, giving convergent (if indirect) evidence
Mechanism is simple and name-agnostic (volume confirms an in-progress move), a reasonable prior for robustness across SPY/QQQ
Decision time (13:00) and hold structure (60 min) are distinct from the lab's existing 11:00 gap-cluster winners, reducing overlap
Moderate thresholds (q85/q70) should support enough trades
